title: Planets speed up when they swing closest to the Sun
body: Kepler’s second law says the line from the Sun to a planet sweeps out **equal areas in equal times**. Near the Sun that line is short, so the planet has to move faster to cover the same area; far away it moves slower. Even Earth’s nearly circular orbit shows it: we travel about 30.3 km/s in early January, when closest to the Sun, and about 29.3 km/s in early July. Newton later showed the law follows from gravity pulling straight toward the Sun.

slides.prompt: In which month is Earth moving fastest along its orbit?
slides.answer: Early January, when it is closest to the Sun
slides.detail: Earth is nearest the Sun around 3 January, moving about 30.3 km/s, and farthest around 4 July, at about 29.3 km/s.

slides.alt: Animation of a brass orrery: a planet on a stretched elliptical orbit is joined to the Sun by an arm that sweeps twelve wedges in equal times, short and fat near the Sun, long and thin far away. The orbit then relaxes to Earth's almost circular one.
slides.music: “Canon in D for Two Renaissance Harps” Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com) · CC BY 4.0

slides.prompt: Stretch the orbit until the planet’s fastest speed is three times its slowest. Watch the equal-time wedges as you go.
slides.takeaway: That takes an eccentricity of 0.5. Each wedge covers the same area in the same time, so close to the Sun the planet has to move faster.

slides.heading: Earth’s speed along its orbit
slides.note: NASA’s Earth fact sheet: 30.29 km/s at most, 29.29 km/s at least

slides.heading: Why it works
slides.text: Gravity pulls a planet straight toward the Sun, along the line joining them. A pull along that line can’t change how fast the line sweeps out area, which is why the law holds for every orbit; physicists call it conservation of angular momentum.

events.text: *Astronomia nova*: the first two laws, from Tycho Brahe’s Mars data.
The third law appears in *Harmonice Mundi*.
His *Epitome* restates the area law for any planet.
Newton’s gravity explains all three laws.

slides.heading: Match Kepler’s laws
slides.explanation: Kepler published the first two laws in 1609 and the third in 1619; Newton later showed all three follow from gravity.
